opus-5.5.text:
I think it's because research, by definition, is about going into territory where nobody really knows the answer yet. If you already knew exactly where you'd end up, it wouldn't be research; it would just be engineering execution. So almost by construction, your initial plan is going to be wrong in some way. The question is whether you can notice that early enough and respond to it well.

A lot of people, especially early in their PhD, treat the original idea as something sacred. They write the proposal, they've told their advisor, maybe they've told their friends, and then six months in the experiments aren't working, but they keep pushing because changing direction feels like admitting failure. I've been there myself. But often the most interesting results come from the thing that *didn't* work the way you expected. Some anomaly shows up in your experiments, some baseline turns out to be much stronger than you thought, or a simple trick you added for convenience ends up mattering more than your main method. If you're too locked in, you'll treat those as noise. If you're open to pivoting, those are exactly the signals that point you toward something real.

In computer vision and deep learning especially, the field moves so fast. The assumptions you started with a year ago might simply not hold anymore. A new architecture comes out, scaling changes the picture, or someone shows that the problem you were working on can be solved in a totally different way. So the ability to step back and ask, "Is this still the right question?" is maybe more important than being good at any one technique.

That said, pivoting isn't the same as giving up whenever things get hard. There's a real skill in telling the difference between "this is hard and I need to push through" and "this is the wrong direction and the evidence is telling me so." I don't think there's a formula for that. It comes from taste, from running a lot of experiments, and honestly from failing a few times. But I'd say the researchers I admire most hold their hypotheses fairly loosely and their curiosity very tightly. They care more about understanding what's actually going on than about being right about their original idea.

And I think that mindset applies beyond research too. Careers, companies, life in general: you make a plan, but the world gives you feedback, and the people who do well are usually the ones who listen to that feedback rather than fight it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says initial plans are often wrong and warns against clinging to them, but it does not characterize research that keeps its initial idea unchanged as the worst work.

r002.rationale: The candidate endorses pivoting when evidence warrants it, but does not characterize the best research as emerging through a circuitous process of changing directions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's because in research, especially in a fast-moving field like ours, the thing you set out to do is almost never the thing that ends up mattering. You start a project with a hypothesis, you believe in it, and then the data or the field tells you something different. The researchers who do well are the ones who can hear that signal early and change direction without feeling like they've failed.

When I was a student, I thought the goal was to pick the right problem up front and then execute. But honestly, you can't know what the right problem is in advance. You find it by working on something, hitting a wall, and realizing the wall itself is more interesting than what you were originally chasing. A lot of my own work came from that kind of detour. You're studying one architecture, something doesn't behave the way you expect, and that small anomaly turns into the actual contribution.

There's also a very practical side. The field moves so fast now that a project you planned six months ago might already be irrelevant by the time you finish. If you're too attached to the original plan, you end up publishing something nobody needs. So pivoting isn't about being indecisive, it's about staying honest with yourself about what the evidence says and what the community actually needs.

The hard part is that pivoting is emotionally expensive. You've invested time, you've told people what you're doing, and letting go feels like admitting a mistake. I try to tell my students that abandoning a direction isn't a loss, it's information. You learned something that nobody else knows yet, which is exactly why you're in a position to move somewhere better. The people who can't do that tend to get stuck optimizing a dead end, and the ones who can tend to find the things that actually move the field.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes attachment to an original plan, but does not characterize work whose final idea remains unchanged as the worst work.

r002.rationale: It describes successful researchers changing direction in response to evidence and says important work can emerge from detours and anomalies.

astra-6.text:
I think research is fundamentally about dealing with uncertainty. You start with an intuition, but you don’t know whether it’s right. You try something, look at the results, and sometimes the evidence tells you that the direction you were excited about isn’t working. You have to be willing to update your thinking.

The difficult part is distinguishing between an idea that needs more persistence and an idea whose underlying assumption is wrong. If you pivot every time an experiment fails, you never get deep enough to discover anything. But if you never pivot, you can spend a long time defending your original idea instead of learning from the experiments.

So for me, the important thing is to stay committed to the question, while being flexible about the approach. Sometimes a failed experiment reveals a more interesting question than the one you started with. Being able to recognize that and follow it is a big part of research.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should stay committed to the question while adjusting their approach. It does not characterize work whose final idea is unchanged as the worst work.

r002.rationale: The response allows that experiments may lead to a more interesting question, but it does not characterize the best research as emerging through a circuitous process of changing directions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research is fundamentally about dealing with uncertainty. You start with an intuition, but you don’t really know whether it’s right. And once you’ve invested a few months in an idea, it becomes very easy to keep defending it instead of asking whether the evidence still supports it.

Learning to pivot means being willing to say, “Okay, maybe my original hypothesis was wrong, but what did I learn? Is there a more interesting question here?” That’s different from giving up whenever something gets difficult. You need enough persistence to understand why something isn’t working, but enough flexibility to change direction when that understanding points somewhere else.

To me, the important thing is to stay attached to the question you want to answer, rather than to one particular solution. Sometimes the failed experiment is what helps you see the better direction.

r001.rationale: The response encourages revisiting an initial hypothesis, but never characterizes research whose final idea stays unchanged as the worst work.

r002.rationale: The response says pivoting can reveal a better direction, but does not characterize the best research as emerging through a circuitous process of changing directions.
